praise (test): Strengthening the two tests that pinned the bug, rather than deleting them, is the right move.

AnUnrecognisedAssignmentStillEndsTheScan asserted RequiresVerification was false, and AThrowingCheckAfterTheFirstAssignmentIsNotAGuard justified the silence in its comment. Both now assert the stricter outcome and keep the original expression check, so they still guard against reading too much. Replaying each fix commit's tests on its parent gives red for the right reason: 3 assertion failures for #297, 6 for #300. The #299 and #298 commits are red at compile time because they reference the new Provenance.SelfReferencing and ScaffoldStatus.TypeIsEnum. Each one is green on its own commit.

issue (blocking): Un cast personnalisé peut retourner null

[P1] IsTheParameterItself retire systématiquement tout CastExpressionSyntax avant de décider qu'une affectation préserve la non-nullité. Or une conversion définie par l'utilisateur peut transformer une chaîne non nulle en null.

Exemple C# valide :

public sealed class ProductCode {
    public static explicit operator ProductCode(string raw)
        => raw.Length < 5 ? null! : new ProductCode();
}

public sealed class Subject {
    public ProductCode Code { get; }
    public Subject(string raw) {
        Code = (ProductCode)raw;
        if (Code is null) throw new ArgumentException("Too short", nameof(raw));
    }
}

CopySources retrouve le cast (ProductCode)raw, IsTheParameterItself le retire et répond true ; le if (Code is null) ne marque donc plus raw comme UnreadGuards. Le générateur peut de nouveau être annoncé comme entièrement inféré alors que le constructeur rejette les chaînes courtes : le P1 que cette correction cherche à éliminer réapparaît.

Ne traiter comme copie directe que les conversions dont la sémantique garantit la conservation de la valeur non nulle (vérifier la conversion résolue par Roslyn, notamment les conversions utilisateur). Une conversion personnalisée doit conserver la marque. Ajouter ce cas aux tests de GuardBoundaryTests.

Confirmed by running the CLI packed from 7507459:

Constructor body Recap
Code = (ProductCode)raw; if (Code is null) throw …, where ProductCode has an explicit operator returning null! for short input raw string Any.String().NonEmpty(), inferred, silent
Value = (object)raw; if (Value is null) throw … inferred, silent (correct: a reference conversion keeps non-null)

A conversion operator that returns null is an unusual design, but it is ordinary C#, and the result is the #297 silence again. The fix is cheap and exact. Strip a cast only when model.GetConversion(cast) is an identity, implicit/explicit reference, or nullable conversion, or more simply whenever !conversion.IsUserDefined. Keep the mark on any user-defined conversion. The ProductCode case belongs in the computed-member theory, and (object)raw in the narrows-nothing one.

Resolved in 47159f2. A cast is now unwrapped only when it does not resolve to a user-defined conversion operator, so (ProductCode)raw keeps the mark.

I wrote the tests first. ProductCode (with its explicit operator returning null!) was added to the computed-member theory, and (object)name to the narrows-nothing theory. On 7507459, only the ProductCode row failed, on the UnreadGuards assertion.

The check had to use the method the cast resolves to (GetSymbolInfo(cast).Symbol is IMethodSymbol { MethodKind: Conversion }). model.GetConversion(cast).IsUserDefined stayed red, because it describes the conversion applied to the cast's result, not the cast itself.

Results now: 735/735 GenAny, 126/126 Cli, 11/11 docs, and the full sweep passes on the unchanged baseline. Spec §5.3 (EN/FR) names the built-in vs user-defined distinction.
